newsitem.title: USA: Appeals court allows Alaska roadwork to go on.
newsitem.headline: Appeals court allows Alaska roadwork to go on.

text.p: A federal appeals court late Wednesday lifted a temporary injunction that had blocked construction of a controverisal road to Prince William Sound, said spokesmen for both sides in the dispute.

The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals notified the state of Alaska, which has been building the road, and environmental groups, which have sued to block it, that work may continue on the motorway to the isolated port of Whittier.

"The governor is very pleased that the 9th Circuit Court has moved so quickly in this manner, which is appropriate given the short construction season in Alaska," said Bob King, press secretary for Democratic Gov. Tony Knowles. "Now that we have been given the proverbial green light, we intend to move forward."
The appeals court in May had issued a temporary order halting construction on the $60 million project, a response to the environmentalists' lawsuit.

The order removing the injunction came a day after the San Francisco-based court heard oral arguments on the dispute in an Anchorage hearing. The three-member appeals panel has yet to issue its ruling on the case, King said.
The five-mile project would convert part of the existing Alaska Railroad spur to Whittier into a one-lane road.
The railroad is the only current on-land access to Whittier, a town of 300 in western Prince William Sound.

Environmentalists say the road, projected to produce 1.4 million annual visits to Whittier in 2015 -- more than 15 times the current level -- would crowd and degrade the sound and areas of the Chugach National Forest.
They have argued that the state and federal governments have neglected to consider upgrades in the existing rail shuttle as an alternative for improving access to Whittier.
According to federal law, roads through federal parks and recreation areas may not be constructed if there is a reasonable alternative that would accomplish the same general transporation goals.
Environmentalist attorney Pat Lavin, who argued the case in court Tuesday, said he was suprised by the swift decision to revoke the injunction.
"I'm more disappointed," said Lavin, of the non-profit firm Trustees for Alaska. "Apparently, this is a pretty good indication they probably want to rule for the state."
Along with Trustees, plaintiffs in the case are the Alaska Centre for the Environment and the Alaska Wilderness Tourism and Recreation Association.

If the formal ruling is in the state's favour, the environmentalists may seek a reconsideration, take the case to a larger panel of appeals judges or seek redress from the U.S. Supreme Court, Lavin said.
King agreed with Lavin that the 9th Circuit's upcoming formal ruling will probably endorse the road's construction.
"Certainly, the signal we got from the 9th Circuit, by their very prompt action, is definitely good for the state's case," he said.
King said contruction equipment that was stilled by May's injunction remains at the site and could be fired up quickly.

The Whittier road would allow motorists to travel one-way, in directions determined by a schedule. Motorists would alternate use of the passageway, which includes two tunnels through the Chugach Mountains, with Alaska Railroad freight trains.
Federal funding is earmarked to cover about three-quarters of the Whittier road's cost.
